USMAN KARAMAT / RESEARCH

what did the
model actually learn?

I study how visual models learn from synthetic data, and what helps that learning transfer to the real world. My research grows out of industrial computer vision: small visual cues, changing camera conditions, and models that must run on edge devices. I use controlled simulation and failure analysis to investigate the evidence these models rely on.

WHERE THE QUESTIONS STARTED

small objects.
real cameras.
unexpected shortcuts.

In industry, I investigate seatbelt and mobile-phone recognition from roadside images of drivers seen through a windshield.

The task depends on small, easily obscured cues. A phone can blend into a hand; a seatbelt can disappear against clothing. Reflections, camera viewpoint, body pose, and crop framing all affect what is visible. A model that performs well on rendered images can still fail at a real camera.

Our system uses a compact shared backbone with separate seatbelt and phone heads. This makes transfer and efficiency inseparable: improvements must ultimately fit within a practical inference budget.

selected research studies

ONE PROGRAMME / THREE QUESTIONS

The first question was about the training data. Following it meant looking more closely at the model—and, eventually, at how we were measuring progress. The work below is ongoing and unpublished. Findings are described qualitatively; public research artifacts will be linked as they become available.

01 / GENERATOR-INDUCED SHORTCUTSEmpirical investigation

when the training data teaches the wrong lesson.

Can a generator make pose or a distractor object a proxy for phone use?

I raised this question after examining the relationship between scene content and class labels. If particular poses or objects appear at different rates across classes, a model may exploit that structure instead of learning to distinguish a phone.

We investigated distractor-containing and distractor-free training sets at matched crop count and class balance. A separate comparison introduced empty-handed negatives in poses used for phone-positive scenes. Keeping these interventions separate helps distinguish object-content effects from pose–label correlations.

Historical comparisons improved performance on development cameras, motivating further study. Later holdout evaluation and a current-recipe distractor rerun did not establish a replicated transfer gain. This makes the conditions under which a shortcut intervention transfers an important part of the question.

That left a more direct question. If changing the training world can change what a model learns, how can we check which part of an image it actually uses?

A SHORTCUT, ILLUSTRATED
phone-positive
phone-negative
different objects + different class frequencies
a convenient correlation
can become the decision rule.

Conceptual illustration; not experiment imagery.

Methodological detail+

Design

I review whether the intended intervention is present in the generated crops, whether class balance and training budget match, and whether an apparent gain holds across the precision–recall curve. Removing a prop, changing its frequency, and adding new poses test different hypotheses.

Interpretation and limits

The earlier findings have limited replication, and some comparisons have augmentation or composition confounds. They support further investigation of the generator’s class structure without establishing a general benefit from removing distractors.

02 / TESTING THE EXPERIMENT ITSELFControlled diagnostic

is it seeing the phone, or everything around it?

How much does the object itself contribute to a correct prediction?

Within the broader failure investigation, we compared phone-region removal with edits to matched regions nearby. The aim was to separate sensitivity to the target object from sensitivity to its surrounding context.

On correctly classified real positives, editing the phone region changed predictions more often than matched context edits. A useful methodological lesson emerged: a grey mask can preserve a phone-shaped cue, so the way an object is removed changes what the experiment can tell us.

I used these findings to guide subsequent data experiments. They also raised the next question: even when a model responds to the right region, does continued training preserve the features that make that evidence useful at a real camera?

COMPARE THE INTERVENTIONS

Edit the phone region and ask whether the prediction changes.

Conceptual illustration; controls are essential to interpretation.

Controls and interpretation+

Design

The diagnostic used inpainting and nearby, wrist, displaced, and background controls. Region size and edit artifacts matter: a prediction change can reflect altered context or an unnatural boundary as well as loss of the object.

Interpretation and limits

The study conditions on correctly classified positives. It establishes sensitivity to the target region within that subset; it does not explain all missed phones or fully isolate a causal mechanism. A training intervention still needs its own controlled comparison.

03 / SYNTHETIC-TO-REAL DRIFTOngoing research

better in simulation. worse at the camera.

Can adaptation to synthetic data strengthen the wrong features, and can a small student retain a teacher’s useful evidence?

A foundation-model teacher improved on synthetic validation while its real-camera performance declined. I proposed backbone adaptation and label ambiguity as possible explanations, and requested comparisons across checkpoints, a frozen-backbone arm, and blinded label reviews.

This led naturally to a second question about distillation. A larger teacher may transfer well, but its advantage must still be learned by a compact student. We explore synthetic-input distillation with supervised class loss, examining the teacher pool and the resulting student separately.

This is where adaptation and distillation meet in my research. I want to understand whether teachers with different failure patterns provide more useful supervision, and which of those differences a compact student can retain.

THE DIRECTION OF THE FINDING
synthetic validationreal-camera evaluation

Schematic trend, not a measured performance chart.

Experimental design and open questions+

Design

For adaptation, compare synthetic and real performance through training, then test specific backbone or data interventions. The original drift study had one seed and a documented schedule bug; several data edits did not resolve the decline, so its mechanism remains open.

Interpretation and limits

For distillation, hold student capacity and training budget fixed while varying supervision. Stronger teacher performance alone does not establish a better student. The research challenge is to identify which differences in teacher behavior survive compression and generalize beyond development cameras.

how I approach a research problem

MEASURE / QUESTION / REVISE

a good result should
survive a better question.

Across these studies, the same habit has become central to my work: move from a failure I can see to an explanation I can test, then let the result change the next question.

01

Locate the failure

I inspect images, error slices, pose coverage, and model disagreements to understand where transfer breaks down. I trace the examples back through labels, cropping, and augmentation before attributing the problem to the model.

02

Isolate the explanation

I formulate competing hypotheses and identify a change that can distinguish them. Comparisons account for dataset size, class balance, training budget, and checkpoint choice; remaining confounds stay explicit.

03

Test and revise

I examine curves, per-camera behavior, and both task heads, then ask whether the finding survives independent evidence. Null results and failed predictions inform the next experiment.

04

Audit the evidence

I check train–evaluation overlap, augmentation provenance, label conventions, and whether the rendered intervention actually arrived, before I trust a number.

Simulation as an experimental instrument

A requested change is useful only if it appears in the rendered data. I review object visibility, masks, crop geometry, and scene composition before interpreting training. For real–synthetic pose comparisons, I use the same estimator on both domains to avoid confusing estimator differences with a coverage gap.

Tools that make reasoning inspectable

To make that process easier to inspect, I work with failure-analysis interfaces, image montages, embedding views, pose audits, and experiment reports. They connect a numerical result to the examples behind it and make the reasoning easier to review. The next question is whether the comparison itself supports a claim about generalization.

My role in the work

I set research priorities, propose and review hypotheses, inspect failure cases, and evaluate whether the evidence supports the conclusion.

I connect scene generation with model evaluation: translating a failure pattern into an experiment brief, reviewing what was generated, and interpreting the resulting comparison. My contributions include raising the distractor hypothesis, directing the broader failure investigation, and proposing explanations for synthetic adaptation drift. Implementation and scoring were done with colleagues and coding agents.

WHAT COUNTS AS EVIDENCE

and how do we know it transfers?

A controlled experiment can tell us something useful about a model. Deciding whether that lesson holds at another camera takes another kind of care.

I examine precision–recall curves to distinguish better discrimination from a change in operating point. Per-site results expose trade-offs hidden by pooled scores, while false-positive rates help compare cameras with different class prevalence. Preserving recall remains central to the application.

Repeated video frames can inflate apparent sample size. I check overlap and near-duplicate structure, and examine group-weighted results where needed. Checkpoint identity, preprocessing, and metric provenance are part of the same audit.

Development cameras help shape hypotheses; a held-out camera serves a different role. I keep that distinction explicit and treat single-seed effects as preliminary. A small numerical gain is not enough to establish a robust improvement, and a result at one new camera leaves broader transfer open.

The programme targets synthetic-only training for the deployment model. That claim requires auditing the full recipe, including augmentation pixels and statistics: a synthetic base dataset can still contain real-derived information. I distinguish those historical recipes from fully real-free variants and keep real-trained diagnostic models separate.

These checks have changed how I read results. A promising score starts a conversation about the evidence; it does not end one. That is also the perspective I bring to the research behind these studies.

questions I want to pursue in a PhD

FUTURE DIRECTIONS
FROM AN INDUSTRIAL PROBLEM TO A RESEARCH AGENDA

the questions I want to take further.

Working through these problems has made me want to study them more deeply. In a PhD, I would like to connect control over the training data with a clearer understanding of what visual models learn and why that learning transfers.

The question that started with a phone behind a windshield has become a broader one for me: can we use simulation to understand what makes visual evidence useful, then carry that understanding into models that work in the real world?

  1. 01

    Can paired scenes predict transfer?

    Matched scenes with and without a target object could reveal whether a model responds to the intended cue. I want to test whether that signal selects more useful synthetic training data than confidence, diversity, or random sampling.

    The key comparison would hold training volume fixed and evaluate the selected data beyond the cameras used to design the score.

  2. 02

    Can we detect shortcuts before training?

    A controllable generator can plant known correlations between labels, objects, poses, and appearance. This offers a way to evaluate whether data audits and slice-discovery methods recover the factors that actually affect transfer.

    I want to connect discovery to intervention: does changing an identified factor produce the predicted change in model behavior?

  3. 03

    Which teacher differences help a student?

    Teachers may achieve similar accuracy while relying on different evidence. I want to investigate whether diversity in their errors and visual sensitivities improves distillation under a fixed student budget.

    This would connect teacher selection to the representations a compact model can retain under domain shift.

A LITTLE CONTEXT

an engineer who kept
asking why.

My background in mechanical engineering at NUST shapes how I approach this problem. I think in terms of physical factors, controlled changes, and experiments that can distinguish competing explanations.

Synthetic scenes let us vary an object, pose, garment, or camera while holding other factors fixed. They also let us create unintended correlations. I am interested in both sides of that control: how it can support useful visual learning, and how it can teach a model the wrong distinction.

The resulting research connects synthetic-to-real transfer, shortcut learning, and evaluation validity. The central question is how to make a model’s success depend on evidence that remains useful outside its training environment.
